lesson.title: Nodes: Every Point Where the Network Connects
lesson.summary: Introduces the network node as the general term for any addressable connection point in a network, a category broad enough to include both end systems and the switching equipment that connects them.
lesson.body:
A computer network can be thought of as a kind of map: a set of points connected by lines. In networking terminology, each of those connection points is called a node. A node is any device that occupies a position in the network's structure and can send, receive, or forward data, while the lines connecting the nodes are the communication links, covered later in this chapter. This is a broader category than the end systems discussed so far. Every end system, your laptop, a web server, a smartphone, is a node. But so is every router and every switch that sits between end systems and forwards their traffic along.

This distinction matters because it separates two different questions that are easy to blur together. "Is this device a node?" simply asks whether it is a connected, addressable point in the network's topology. "Is this device an end system?" asks something more specific: whether it is one of the endpoints actually originating or consuming data, as opposed to relaying someone else's. Every end system is a node, but not every node is an end system. A router forwarding traffic between two networks is very much a node, it has an identifiable place in the network and connects to other devices through links, but it is not an end system, because applications do not run on it and it is not the ultimate source or destination of the data it handles.

Thinking of a network as nodes connected by links also explains why network diagrams look the way they do. When an engineer sketches a network, whether on a whiteboard or in specialized software, they draw circles for nodes and lines for links, exactly the way you might draw a map of cities connected by roads. Some nodes on that diagram, like end system computers, represent where data starts and finishes its journey. Other nodes, like routers, represent the intersections where the data's path gets decided and it gets sent onward.

Consider a small home network as a worked example. The laptop, the smart TV, and the printer in your house are each nodes, and each is also an end system. The WiFi router that connects them to each other and to the internet is also a node, since it has a defined position that other devices connect to, but it is not an end system, because it exists to forward traffic between your devices and the wider internet rather than to be the traffic's source or destination itself. If you counted every node in your home network, you would count your devices and your router together. If you counted only the end systems, you would leave the router out.

Understanding nodes as the general category sets up the next two sections cleanly. The network edge is built from end system nodes and the links that reach them, while the network core is built from the switching and routing nodes, like the router in this example, that interconnect everything else.
